# Dental disorders

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Emergency medicine > Head and neck disorders > Dental disorders*

[Original Article Link](/library/is0Juh)

---

## Summary

<u>Tooth decay</u> (<u>dental caries</u>) is the progressive destruction of dental tissue following <u>enamel</u> damage by acid-producing bacteria in <u>dental plaque</u>. Manifestations include <u>dentalgia</u> and <u>halitosis</u>. Diagnosis is usually clinical and can involve imaging (e.g., <u>x-ray</u>). Treatment often includes <u>caries</u> excavation and surface restoration.




<u>Periodontal disease</u> includes various inflammatory conditions, such as <u>gingivitis</u>, <u>periodontitis</u>, <u>pericoronitis</u>, and <u>acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis</u>, that affect <u>tooth</u>-supporting structures, including the <u>gingiva</u>, <u>periodontal ligament</u>, and/or alveolar bone. Management is based on severity but often includes oral hygiene measures, topical <u>antiseptics</u>, systemic <u>antibiotics</u>, and/or referral for <u>dental plaque</u> <u>debridement</u>.




Dental <u>abscesses</u> can arise from infections and/or trauma to <u>dental pulp</u> and/or periodontal tissue and often extend locally. Clinical features include <u>dentalgia</u>, gingival swelling and <u>erythema</u>, and <u>purulent</u> discharge. Signs of regional and/or systemic progression requiring urgent management include <u>dysphagia</u>, facial <u>erythema</u>, and <u>fever</u>. Treatment can include <u>incision and drainage</u>, dental extraction, and <u>antibiotics</u>.




<u>Dental injuries</u> can involve <u>dental avulsion</u> (complete displacement from the socket), <u>dental subluxation and luxation</u> (injury to the <u>periodontal ligament</u>, and <u>dental fracture</u>. Management depends on the injury type and extent and can include manual replantation or reduction, dental splinting, <u>antibiotics</u>, root canal, and surface restoration.




<u>Malocclusion</u> is a deviation from the ideal <u>tooth</u> position that affects dental contact during biting. It is usually asymptomatic but can cause symptoms in pronounced cases. Management includes orthodontic correction and <u>jaw</u> repositioning.

---

## Tooth decay

* Definitions

* <u>Dental caries</u>: the progressive destruction of dental tissue following damage to the <u>enamel</u> by acid produced by bacteria in <u>dental plaque</u>

* Pulpitis: inflammation of the <u>dental pulp</u>  [[4]](/library/OQ1Iwg0)

* <u>Epidemiology</u>
* <u>Prevalence</u> of untreated <u>dental caries</u>

* Children 5–19 years of age: 13.2%

* Adults 20–64 years of age: ∼ 24%

* Etiology

* Pathogens: <u>Streptococcus mutans</u>, S. mitis, <u>Actinomyces</u>, <u>Lactobacillus</u>

* <u>Risk factors</u>

* Presence of specific microorganisms in <u>dental plaque</u> (e.g., <u>S. mutans</u>, <u>Lactobacillus</u>)

* Patient factors include:

* Poor oral hygiene

* High-sugar diet

* <u>Xerostomia</u>, e.g., due to <u>Sjogren syndrome</u>

* Pathophysiology: oral bacteria metabolize <u>carbohydrates</u> → acid production (e.g., <u>lactic acid</u>) → demineralization of <u>tooth</u> <u>enamel</u>

* Clinical features

* <u>Tooth</u> <u>pain</u>

* Possibly <u>bad breath</u>

* Diagnostics

* Inspection of the <u>oral cavity</u> with a mouth mirror: change in <u>enamel</u> (e.g., <u>enamel</u> breakdown, surface discoloration)

* The <u>teeth</u> can be probed with dental instruments to check for soft areas.

* Bitewing <u>radiography</u>: Carious lesions appear <u>radiolucent</u>.

* Differential diagnosis

* <u>Dental fluorosis</u>

* Dental hypomineralization

* Dental <u>hypoplasia</u>

* Treatment: depends on the size and extent of the lesion

* Very small lesion in which remineralization is still possible: The application of <u>fluoride</u> gel, varnishes, pit, and/or <u>fissure</u> sealant usually suffices.

* Lesions that involve hard tissues but do not involve the pulp: <u>caries</u> excavation and restoration of the dental surface

* Lesions that involve both <u>enamel</u> and <u>dentin</u> in proximity to the pulp: <u>indirect pulp capping</u>

* Lesions that involve <u>enamel</u>, <u>dentin</u>, and pulp: root canal treatment, followed by extracoronal restoration

* Complications: mostly caused by inflammation of the pulp 

* Apical <u>periodontitis</u>

* <u>Periapical abscess</u>

* <u>Periostitis</u>, <u>osteomyelitis</u>

* Prevention

* Proper oral hygiene

* Use of toothpaste supplemented with <u>fluoride</u>





![Dental caries](media/nmbck2msqfqj2u17z1vtmo5u.jpg)

## Periodontal disease

Consists of various inflammatory conditions that affect the supporting tissues of the <u>teeth</u>, including the <u>gingiva</u>, <u>periodontal ligament</u>, and/or alveolar bone [[4]](/library/OQ1Iwg0)[[5]](/library/f41kiS0)




### Etiology [[5]](/library/f41kiS0)[[6]](/library/gQ1Fvg0)[[7]](/library/g41FiS0)




* Caused by bacteria in <u>dental plaque</u> (see “Etiology” in “<u>Tooth decay</u>”)

* <u>Risk factors</u>

* Lifestyle factors: e.g., smoking, poor oral hygiene

* Systemic conditions: e.g., <u>HIV infection</u>, <u>diabetes</u>

* <u>Gingival hyperplasia</u>: e.g., <u>drug-induced gingival overgrowth</u>





### Disease spectrum [[4]](/library/OQ1Iwg0)[[5]](/library/f41kiS0)[[6]](/library/gQ1Fvg0)[[8]](/library/35YSPp)




* Gingivitis: reversible inflammation of the <u>gums</u>

* Clinical features: <u>gum</u> swelling and <u>erythema</u>; bleeding with brushing and/or flossing

* Management: Encourage <u>smoking cessation</u>, improved oral hygiene, and routine dental care.

* Periodontitis: a nonreversible inflammatory condition involving the <u>gingiva</u>, <u>periodontal ligament</u>, and/or alveolar bone

* <u>Risk factors</u>

* <u>Dental plaque</u>, <u>dental calculus</u>, <u>caries</u>

* <u>Tooth</u> positioning

* Trauma

* Medications (e.g., <u>nifedipine</u>, <u>cyclosporine</u>, <u>phenytoin</u>)

* Systemic conditions (e.g., <u>diabetes mellitus</u>)

* <u>Puberty</u>, <u>pregnancy</u>, <u>OCPs</u>

* <u>Immunocompromised state</u> (e.g., <u>HIV</u>, <u>leukemia</u>)

* Clinical features

* Gingival <u>erythema</u>, swelling, and bleeding

* Recession of the gingival margin

* <u>Halitosis</u>

* Increased <u>tooth</u> mobility

* Management: Refer all patients to a dentist for evaluation and treatment including the removal of <u>dental plaque</u> and <u>dental tartar</u>

* Pericoronitis: inflammation and/or infection of the <u>gingiva</u> at the site of <u>tooth</u> eruption  [[9]](/library/SQ1yvg0)[[10]](/library/J41s4S0)

* Clinical features: <u>pain</u> and localized gingival swelling, typically at the site of the third mandibular molar

* Management

* Mild disease: antibacterial mouth rinse with <u>chlorhexidine</u> DOSAGE or with <u>hydrogen peroxide</u> DOSAGE [[6]](/library/gQ1Fvg0)[[8]](/library/35YSPp)

* Severe disease: systemic <u>antibiotic</u> treatment with <u>penicillin</u> DOSAGE OR <u>clindamycin</u> DOSAGE [[4]](/library/OQ1Iwg0)[[8]](/library/35YSPp)

* Refer all patients to a dentist or oral <u>surgeon</u> for local <u>debridement</u> and consideration of <u>tooth</u> extraction.

* Acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis (<u>ANUG</u>): a polymicrobial gingival infection characterized by tissue <u>necrosis</u>

* Clinical features

* Gingival inflammation with white <u>plaques</u>, <u>ulcerations</u>, and bleeding

* Fetid breath

* Pseudomembranes may be present.

* May extend to the <u>tonsils</u> and <u>pharynx</u> (see “<u>Vincent angina</u>”)

* Management

* Refer all patients to a dentist for evaluation and treatment including <u>debridement</u> and/or topical <u>antiseptic</u> therapy

* Urgently consult ENT and/or oral <u>surgery</u> for patients with pharyngeal involvement and/or systemic symptoms (e.g., <u>fever</u>).





### Dental infection red flags [[6]](/library/gQ1Fvg0)[[10]](/library/J41s4S0)




The following <u>red flags</u> suggest progression to deep tissue or systemic <u>complications of periodontal and dental infections</u> that require urgent management:




* Swelling of the face, neck, and/or floor of the mouth

* Facial <u>erythema</u>

* Regional <u>lymphadenopathy</u>

* <u>Trismus</u>

* Difficulty <u>swallowing</u> or handling secretions

* <u>Dyspnea</u> and/or <u>airway</u> compromise

* <u>Headache</u> or stiff neck

* <u>Fever</u>





> [!TIP]
> In patients presenting with periodontal <u>pain</u> or bleeding, provide appropriate <u>supportive care for periodontal disorders</u>.




> [!WARNING]
> In patients with <u>red flags for progression of periodontal infections</u>, consider systemic <u>antibiotics</u> and urgent referral to <u>surgery</u> for management of a possible <u>deep neck infection</u>.

## Dental abscess

### Overview




* Definition:  the accumulation of <u>purulent</u> fluid within the <u>dental pulp</u> or periodontal tissue [[10]](/library/J41s4S0)

* Etiology [[10]](/library/J41s4S0)

* <u>Dental caries</u>

* Poor oral hygiene

* Trauma

* Unsuccessful root canal treatment

* Types [[4]](/library/OQ1Iwg0)

* Periapical abscess

* Most common type

* <u>Tooth decay</u> or trauma → bacterial infection in the pulp of the <u>tooth</u> → collection of <u>pus</u> at the apex of the dental root

* The infection becomes visible when it extends through the alveolar bone (e.g., via a <u>fistula</u>) to the surrounding tissue.  [[11]](/library/7Sb4at)

* <u>Periodontal abscess</u>

* Second most common type

* <u>Periodontitis</u> or impaction of foreign objects (e.g., food, dental floss) → bacterial infection deep in the periodontal pocket → collection of <u>pus</u> between the <u>teeth</u> and <u>gingiva</u>

* The affected <u>tooth</u> may be mobile.





> [!TIP]
> Periodontal <u>abscesses</u> originate in the periodontal tissue; the <u>tooth</u> itself may be healthy. Periapical <u>abscesses</u> originate in the <u>dental pulp</u> and always involve the <u>tooth</u>.




> [!WARNING]
> Dental infections can spread locally to the <u>gums</u> and alveolar bone and to regional structures including the deep neck spaces and intracranial sinuses (see “Complications”).




### Clinical features




* Severe <u>pain</u> can generally be elicited with palpation.

* Swelling and <u>erythema</u> of the surrounding <u>mucosa</u>

* <u>Purulent</u> discharge from the <u>gum</u> line may be seen.

* The affected <u>tooth</u> may be discolored and/or show <u>enamel</u> breaks.





![Dental abscess](media/cja0tke09oloba1ax3u1wuu5.jpg)

Dental abscess

![Dental abscess](media/cffyp8v50x9lwpraskmvkm23.jpg)

Dental abscess




### Diagnostics [[8]](/library/35YSPp)[[10]](/library/J41s4S0)




* An oral examination is usually sufficient to make a diagnosis.

* Obtain diagnostic studies if <u>red flags for progression of dental abscess</u> are present.

* <u>Laboratory studies</u>: <u>CBC</u> (may show <u>leukocytosis</u>, <u>neutrophilia</u>)  [[8]](/library/35YSPp)

* Imaging: <u>x-ray</u>, CT, or <u>MRI</u> of the head and neck

* To assess for possible spread to the neck and/or sinus cavities

* May show subcutaneous air (sign of <u>necrosis</u>) and/or <u>deviation of the trachea</u>

* See also “Diagnostics” in “<u>Deep neck infections</u>.”





### Management [[8]](/library/35YSPp)[[9]](/library/SQ1yvg0)[[10]](/library/J41s4S0)




* Consult a dentist or oral <u>surgeon</u> for <u>abscess</u> <u>incision and drainage</u>, and, if necessary, removal of the affected <u>tooth</u>.

* Start <u>empiric antibiotic treatment</u> for systemic symptoms (e.g., <u>fever</u>) or if surgical intervention is delayed.  [[8]](/library/35YSPp)[[9]](/library/SQ1yvg0)[[10]](/library/J41s4S0)[[12]](/library/Zq1ZC30)

* Adults

* <u>Penicillin</u> DOSAGE OR <u>metronidazole</u> DOSAGE  [[8]](/library/35YSPp)[[10]](/library/J41s4S0)

* <u>Amoxicillin/clavulanate</u> DOSAGE [[8]](/library/35YSPp)

* Children 

* First-line: <u>amoxicillin</u> DOSAGE [[13]](/library/Cedqa60)

* <u>Penicillin</u> <u>allergy</u>: <u>azithromycin</u> DOSAGE or <u>doxycycline</u> DOSAGE  [[13]](/library/Cedqa60)

* Provide <u>supportive care for dental disorders</u>.





> [!TIP]
> Manage dental <u>abscesses</u> with <u>incision and drainage</u>; <u>antibiotic therapy</u> alone is not sufficient. [[4]](/library/OQ1Iwg0)[[14]](/library/K41U4S0)




> [!WARNING]
> If <u>red flags for dental infection progression</u> are present, consult maxillofacial or oral <u>surgery</u> immediately.




![Dental abscess](media/cja0tke09oloba1ax3u1wuu5.jpg)

Dental abscess

![Dental abscess](media/cffyp8v50x9lwpraskmvkm23.jpg)

Dental abscess

## Dental injuries

Emergency management of <u>dental injuries</u> includes assessing for concurrent injury, preserving <u>tooth</u> viability, and infection prevention. Follow-up care with a dentist is always required. [[9]](/library/SQ1yvg0)




### Dental avulsion [[8]](/library/35YSPp)[[9]](/library/SQ1yvg0)[[15]](/library/4Q13wg0)




* Definition: the complete displacement of a <u>tooth</u> from its socket

* Management

* Replant a <u>permanent tooth</u> as quickly as possible. ;  [[8]](/library/35YSPp) 

* Handle the <u>tooth</u> by the crown only.

* Rinse off debris with saline (do not scrub or sterilize).

* Gently reduce the <u>tooth</u> into the correct <u>anatomical position</u>.

* <u>Splint</u> the <u>tooth</u> in the correct position with wax or dental cement.

* Begin <u>antibiotic prophylaxis</u>: <u>doxycycline</u> DOSAGE for adults, <u>penicillin</u> DOSAGE for children < 12 years of age [[8]](/library/35YSPp)[[15]](/library/4Q13wg0)

* Provide <u>tetanus prophylaxis</u> if indicated. [[15]](/library/4Q13wg0)

* If unable to replant the <u>tooth</u>:

* Place the <u>tooth</u> in a physiologic storage medium: <u>Hanks balanced salt solution</u> or milk

* Notify the dentist or oral <u>surgeon</u> immediately.

* If an <u>avulsed tooth</u> is unaccounted for:

* Examine for deep displacement into the tissue or socket.

* Obtain a <u>chest x-ray</u> to rule out <u>aspiration</u>.





> [!WARNING]
> Avulsion of a <u>permanent tooth</u> is a dental emergency. Manual replantation is indicated as soon as possible, followed by urgent referral to a dentist. [[15]](/library/4Q13wg0)




> [!WARNING]
> Do not replant <u>primary teeth</u>. [[9]](/library/SQ1yvg0)




### Dental subluxation and luxation [[8]](/library/35YSPp)[[9]](/library/SQ1yvg0)[[16]](/library/PQ1Wwg0)




* Definition: partial or complete disruption of the <u>periodontal ligament</u>, resulting in <u>tooth</u> mobility within the socket

* Subluxation: the <u>tooth</u> is mobile but remains in the correct <u>anatomical position</u>

* Luxation: displacement of the <u>tooth</u> into a nonanatomical position

* Management

* Consult dentistry.

* Gently reduce the <u>tooth</u> to the correct <u>anatomical position</u>, if necessary.

* <u>Splint</u> the <u>tooth</u> in the correct position with wax or dental cement.

* Provide <u>supportive care for dental disorders</u>.

* Obtain serial dental radiographs to assess for evidence of a root <u>fracture</u>.





### Dental fracture [[8]](/library/35YSPp)[[9]](/library/SQ1yvg0)[[16]](/library/PQ1Wwg0)




* Definition: a partial or complete interruption in the continuity of a <u>tooth</u>

* Classification and clinical characteristics: Dental <u>fractures</u> may involve the crown, root, and/or alveolar bone.

* <u>Enamel</u> infraction: <u>enamel</u> <u>crack</u> without disruption of <u>tooth</u> structure

* Crown <u>fracture</u>

* Ellis I (limited to <u>enamel</u>): painless, no bleeding

* Ellis II (<u>dentin</u> is exposed): <u>fracture</u> site appears yellow, no or minimal bleeding

* Ellis III (pulp is exposed): <u>fracture</u> site appears pink, heat and cold <u>sensitivity</u>, possible bleeding

* Root <u>fracture</u>: The <u>tooth</u> is mobile, tender to palpation, and often bleeds.

* Alveolar bone <u>fracture</u>: may cause segmental displacement with movement in multiple adjacent <u>teeth</u>

* Management

* Consult dentistry: Urgency is based on the class of <u>fracture</u>.  [[8]](/library/35YSPp)

* Obtain imaging (e.g., <u>radiography</u>, CT) if a <u>fracture</u> of the dental root or alveolar bone is suspected. [[16]](/library/PQ1Wwg0)

* Control bleeding and <u>pain</u>; see “<u>Supportive care for dental disorders</u>.”

* Consider the application of dental cement (<u>calcium</u> hydroxide paste) to Ellis II and Ellis III <u>fractures</u> pending dental consult. [[9]](/library/SQ1yvg0)

* <u>Antibiotics</u> are not typically required. [[9]](/library/SQ1yvg0)

* Definitive management

* <u>Enamel</u> infraction: sealing with bonding resin in severe cases

* Crown <u>fracture</u>

* Ellis I and II: <u>tooth</u> fragment replantation or <u>tooth</u> edge smoothing

* Ellis III: pulp therapy, possible root canal

* Root <u>fracture</u>: splinting, possible root canal

* Alveolar bone <u>fracture</u>: repositioning and splinting

## Malocclusion

* Definition: any deviation from ideal <u>tooth</u> positioning that leads to irregular contact between the upper and lower <u>teeth</u> when the <u>jaw</u> is closed

* Types: The most common forms are <u>anterior</u> crowding, vertical overbite, and <u>sagittal</u> overjet. [[17]](/library/MtcMVV0)

* Clinical features

* Usually asymptomatic

* In severe cases: discomfort when biting or chewing, frequent biting of cheeks or <u>tongue</u>, speech problems

* Management: : correction of deviated <u>teeth</u> and <u>jaw</u> positions through orthodontic treatment (e.g., <u>braces</u>) to achieve proper occlusion

* Prognosis: Whether orthodontic correction of dental alignment has a positive effect on dental health is still subject to debate. [[18]](/library/ntc7VV0)





![Malocclusion in pediatric obstructive sleep apnea (OSA)](media/lf251065tf97tq1igopbhbjq.jpg)

Malocclusion in pediatric obstructive sleep apnea (OSA)

## Differential diagnoses

### Nonodontogenic causes of orofacial <u>pain</u> [[9]](/library/SQ1yvg0)[[19]](/library/BN1zWh0)




* <u>Myofascial pain syndrome</u>

* <u>Temporomandibular joint dysfunction</u>

* <u>Trigeminal neuralgia</u>

* <u>Temporal arteritis</u>

* <u>Peritonsillar abscess</u>

* <u>Langerhans cell histiocytosis</u>

* <u>Sinusitis</u>

* <u>Otitis media</u>

* <u>Headache</u> syndromes: e.g., <u>migraine</u>, <u>cluster headache</u>

* <u>Myocardial</u> <u>ischemia</u>  [[19]](/library/BN1zWh0)





The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.
